themes.definition: Requirements that a person checks, validates, interprets or approves AI outputs before or while they are used, including which cases must reach a human and how officials should treat outputs.
themes.what_is_set_out: The Playbook (UK174) tells end-users to 'check that outputs are accurate, non-discriminatory, non-harmful' and lawful, says with 'must' that human-in-the-loop processes validate output 'in situations with high impact or risk', that outputs about individuals be treated as a 'statistically informed guess', and that a human must review an agent's action before it is carried out. The DWP policy (UK190) is the one binding departmental policy in the cell that puts output checking on every user and supplier ('Users must check the accuracy, reliability, and credibility of AI output'), but only 'to the best of their ability' and with no method. UK099 asks that 'someone' verifies LLM outputs for incorrect information and bias, UK010 (Ofgem) asks for roles 'accountable for monitoring, validating and interpreting any AI-generated results', UK268 has auditors confirm human-in-the-loop validation where decisions have significant impacts, and NAO commits itself to 'validation, testing and human oversight'. AI_Insights says which cases reach a human: depending on the use case 'some or all of the time'; 'whenever your AI model is making decisions that your organisation would normally expect to account for'; edge cases; uncertain or sensitive classifier results; sampled judgements (about 10%, or 1,000 records for very large collections, per coder notes); every code commit and merge; and in one KIM use the AI's summary is used to check the human's retention decision rather than the reverse. The ATRS template (UK087) asks bodies to disclose 'When and how does a person review the tool's output? How is that review assessed / assured?', but no document says how reviewers should judge accuracy, what training they need, or what happens if review is skipped.
themes.holders: 'You' as end-user (UK174); users and suppliers and their third parties (UK190); 'someone' (UK099); teams and individuals in roles set by organisations using AI (UK010); human reviewers (UK268, UK071); KIM professionals and teams, trained reviewers, sensitivity reviewers, developers and peer reviewers (AI_Insights); NAO for itself; the organisation completing the ATRS record.
themes.binding: DWP 'must' as departmental policy, qualified by 'to the best of their ability'; UK174 'must' (038, 084) in non-statutory guidance; otherwise 'should', 'need', 'can', 'required' depending on use case. The ATRS asks only for disclosure. No consequences stated for skipping review.
themes.checks: Trigger: each use (UK190 [inference]); high-impact or high-risk situations; before an agent's action; decisions the organisation would expect to account for; edge cases and uncertain classifier scores; every commit and merge of AI-assisted code; before scaling (sample review). Compared against: legal provisions, guidelines, policies and the provider's terms of use (UK174, 037); benchmarks set in discovery (AI_Insights KIM); otherwise not stated. Metric or threshold: accuracy, reliability, credibility, bias, misinformation; sample sizes of about 10% or 1,000 records; UK071's example of more than 80% of sampled outputs rated acceptable; no general threshold. Who: users, suppliers, KIM professionals, trained reviewers, peers; often 'someone' or not stated. What happens with the result: correct, approve or intervene; refine prompts; adjust the solution until it meets benchmarks; otherwise not stated.

themes.theme: Over-reliance on AI and loss of human skills
themes.definition: Requirements to assess whether people will over-trust AI outputs, or lose the skills needed to check them, override them or recover when the tool fails.
themes.what_is_set_out: Four documents raise this, all as questions or recommendations. UK133 asks evaluators whether users 'become overly reliant on the AI tool or overly trusting of its outputs', even where the tool's limited accuracy is presented to them; UK010 (Ofgem) recommends human oversight from the earliest stage while considering 'both overconfidence and a lack of trust in the AI components' (coder note), and asks that the loss of internal security skills from AI-based security tools be considered. UK071 is the most specific: organisations 'should assess the risk of skill loss' where staff are 'safety backstops (e.g. validating AI outputs)' or manual recovery may be needed, and teams should test whether non-technical users 'can tell when the AI is hallucinating, biased, or off-topic'. UK266 asks audit committees whether 'overreliance on automation and loss of institutional knowledge' are being identified and mitigated. [inference] This theme qualifies the human-review theme: several documents rely on people to check outputs while recognising that the checker may defer to the tool, but none says how the quality of human review is to be measured.
themes.holders: Evaluators (UK133); not stated, nearest stakeholders (UK010); organisations and teams (UK071); the organisation answering audit committee questions (UK266).
themes.checks: Trigger: when scoping an evaluation (UK133); from the earliest stage (UK010); on introducing AI tools; ongoing. Compared against: not stated. Metric or threshold: not stated; UK071 suggests user tests of whether people can spot hallucination or bias. Who: evaluators; organisations; teams. What happens with the result: not stated beyond 'mitigated' (UK266).

themes.theme: Controls on AI coding assistants and AI-generated code
themes.definition: Requirements on developers who use AI coding assistants or LLM-generated code: understanding and peer review of the code, checks on dependencies and tool versions, protection of production systems and secrets, and avoiding reliance on any one tool.
themes.what_is_set_out: The Playbook (UK174) says to 'Treat all LLM-generated code as inherently insecure' and never to put it into production without a code review. AI_Insights develops this into a set of developer duties: treat assistants 'as if they are a programmer who lacks experience', 'only commit code changes that you understand' and take 'sole responsibility for any changes'; subject merges to the main branch to human peer review by one or more peers; keep commits small so reviewers are not overloaded; and check dependency versions 'against trusted sources' because hallucinated version numbers can be exploited (coder note). It also asks for multi-layered vulnerability scanning rather than reliance on the vendor's own mitigation (coder note), monitoring of plugin and model versions with changelogs read for breaking or licence changes, a production environment insulated from development changes, no secrets in development environments, checks that beta features are not covered by different data-collection terms, and no dependency of the end product on the tool used. Bias is left to the developer: assistants 'will not actively recognise or flag bias'. These are the most concrete human-review rules in the cell, with a clear trigger (every commit and merge), but they sit in guidance with 'should', 'need to' or imperatives and no stated consequence.
themes.holders: Developers in HMG ('you'); one or more peer reviewers; 'you as risk owner' for insulating production; development teams.
themes.binding: Non-binding guidance: imperatives ('Always', 'Make sure'), 'should never', 'need to', 'require'. The only consequence named is accepting 'the risk of frequent breakage' if a build relies on a specific prompt response (404).
themes.checks: Trigger: every commit and every merge to the main branch; whenever an assistant introduces a dependency; on tool, plugin or model updates. Compared against: trusted sources (dependency versions); the organisation's policies; the changelog. Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: the developer; one or more peers. What happens with the result: code is not committed or merged unless understood and reviewed [inference]; production is protected from unchecked changes.

quotes.location: AI Insights: AI Coding Assistants for developers…

quotes.location: AI Insights: AI Coding Assistants for developers…

quotes.location: AI Insights: AI Coding Assistants for developers…

themes.theme: Agentic and autonomous systems: profiling, testing paths and human control
themes.definition: Requirements specific to AI systems that act with some autonomy (agents, agentic workflows and RAG, multi-model systems): profiling their behaviour, testing execution paths and out-of-range conditions, validating agents before live use, keeping audit trails and keeping humans in control.
themes.what_is_set_out: AI_Insights carries almost all of this. It asks teams to 'profile our systems so that we know how they behave under different conditions' and to keep profiling in production to compare expected with achieved performance; to go beyond unit testing to system and integration tests that 'demonstrate multiple execution pathways'; to make testing of rare and out-of-range cases 'mandatory' and build guardrails; to deploy only 'fully-tested and targeted versions of frameworks'; to keep audit logs of state changes and function calls as 'standard practice in any agentic system'; to set termination criteria for iterative runs; and to validate a user-built agent ('entity') as safe before it runs on live or production data. It names 'the system designer' as responsible for knowing and controlling the system's profile, recommends against building one's own agent frameworks, and asks that agentic systems manage risk 'at a fundamental architectural level'. The Playbook (UK174) requires, with 'must', a human present to review an agent's action before it is carried out; UK268 asks that interactions between multiple models be assessed for amplified risk; UK071 asks for evaluation 'during prolonged unattended operation and edge cases', including checks of human handover triggers (coder note). 'Must' is frequent, but in non-binding guidance, and the conditions that should trigger a hand-over to a human are not stated.
themes.holders: 'We' or not stated (AI_Insights), nearest the system designer; entity creators and owners; 'you' or the organisation (UK174); not stated (UK268, UK071).
themes.binding: Non-binding guidance: 'must', 'should be mandatory', 'should', 'not recommended'. No consequences stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: during development; before running on live or production data; on framework upgrades or a change of underlying LLM; ongoing in production; on every request (audit log). Compared against: expected conditions and expected performance; the rules, guidelines and guardrails 'we have established' (entity approval, 449); system objectives. Metric or threshold: profiling measures such as supported parallel requests, concurrent users and cost of execution paths (coder note to 410); otherwise not stated. Who: system designer; entity creator; not stated. What happens with the result: guardrails built; approval for live use (the approval itself is coded elsewhere); human review before action (UK174).

themes.definition: Delivery arrangements for when an AI tool misbehaves or is retired: fail-safe design, ways to slow down or stop, fallbacks and rollback, decommissioning when harms are found, secure disposal, and updating records on retirement.
themes.what_is_set_out: UK071 states the principle most strongly: 'When AI does fail, it must fail safely', with fallbacks such as handing off to a human (coder note), an Operational Acceptance Test that covers kill switches and undo, and a plan for decommissioning. UK099 recommends building in 'ways for the system to slow down or stop' and asks whether there is a process for decommissioning with minimal impact on end users; UK010 (Ofgem) mentions 'wraparound systems and guardrails' to keep a system in a safe state and asks users of AI to assess failure modes. UK268 asks for change management with fallback mechanisms and for security incident procedures 'including rollback or decommissioning if necessary'; the Playbook (UK174) says, with 'must', that mechanisms be in place to change or decommission AI systems 'if unacceptable risks or harms are identified'. UK010 and AI_Insights cover secure disposal of systems and sample data, AI_Insights recommends a back-up copy so that roll-back is available if errors are made, and UK085 requires the ATRS record to be updated to 'Retired'. Who decides to stop is generally not stated in these delivery passages [inference: that decision sits in the Decision-making row].
themes.holders: 'You' (UK174, UK099); not stated (UK268, UK071); stakeholders and users of AI (UK010); KIM professionals (AI_Insights); the responsible team (UK085).
themes.binding: Non-statutory. 'Must' in UK174 (041) and as a UK071 principle (377); otherwise 'should', 'consider', 'possible control'. The ATRS retirement update is required by policy for bodies in mandatory scope.
themes.checks: Trigger: failure or unexpected behaviour; security incidents; unacceptable risks or harms; end of use. Compared against: not stated. Metric or threshold: not stated; UK071 gives an example fallback coverage of 95% or more (coder note to 364). Who: not stated. What happens with the result: safe state, hand-off to a human, rollback, decommissioning, secure disposal, record marked 'Retired'.

themes.definition: Requirements or suggestions to keep machine logs of what goes into and comes out of an AI tool in use (prompts, outputs, conversation history, agent actions, errors and access) for audit, debugging, security and later analysis.
themes.what_is_set_out: The Playbook (UK174) says bodies 'can' log and audit all interactions with a model, and recommends logging 'all prompts sent to a model' with ongoing audits for prompt injection. UK099 says transparency 'may also include an audit log of the prompts and outputs generated by AI systems', and says with 'must' that teams keep audit trails of who has access to data and why. UK071 asks teams to test that conversation history or prompt logs can be retrieved ('that’s your audit trail'; example metric: all responses linked to logged prompts, per coder note) and to log all AI errors. AI_Insights asks that all model inputs and outputs be logged during development and testing, recommends audit logs of agent state changes, output auditing that logs all outputs for retrospective bias analysis, access logging and prompt auditing, and says log storage and privacy 'must be considered during system design'. UK136 asks for process logs across the project life cycle, UK190 (DWP) reserves a power to monitor use of its systems, and the ATRS template (UK087) asks whether operational data such as 'user interaction logs' are stored, without requiring them. No document makes logging of prompts and outputs in live use mandatory, sets a retention period, or says who reviews the logs.
themes.holders: 'You' or teams (UK174, UK099, AI_Insights); DWP (power to monitor); the team (UK071); the organisation completing the ATRS record; central government departments and project teams (UK136).
themes.binding: Mostly non-binding: 'can', 'should', 'may', 'consider'. 'Must' in UK099 for access audit trails (226, non-statutory guidance) and in AI_Insights only for considering log storage (532). DWP's 'may monitor' is a power under departmental policy. ATRS asks for disclosure only.
themes.checks: Trigger: every request or interaction; during development and testing; ongoing. Compared against: for prompt-injection audits, signs of attack; otherwise not stated. Metric or threshold: UK071 example of full prompt traceability; otherwise not stated. Who: not stated. What happens with the result: audit trail; blocking users found responsible for prompt injection (UK174, 082); retrospective bias analysis; performance improvement during development.

themes.theme: Documentation and record-keeping across the life cycle
themes.definition: Requirements to keep internal records of how an AI tool was designed, built, tested and used, who decided what and on what evidence, including model and data cards, inventories of AI use, records of evaluations and records of equality consideration.
themes.what_is_set_out: The strongest wording is in UK099, which says with 'must' that teams 'record who is responsible for each part of the system, including suppliers' and keep clear records showing how the system 'was designed, developed, tested and implemented'. The Playbook (UK174) recommends an internal AI and machine learning systems inventory 'in addition to' the ATRS (coder note), up-to-date internal records, and evaluation and auditing structures that track data provenance and design decisions. UK268 lists documentation as expected controls: test results and corrective actions, data, system and audit cards, fairness metrics with their rationale, the assumptions behind evaluations, and comprehensive model records. UK010 (Ofgem) asks for records explaining 'the basis of AI decisions in a proportionate manner' so that stakeholders can review input and assure processing; UK071 suggests datasheets and verifying traceability records; AI_Insights asks KIM teams to record the results of model runs on sample sets. The EHRC checklist (UK216) cites case law that it is good practice to record how equality was considered, and asks bodies to identify 'if and how you (or others on your behalf) use AI'. These records are mainly for internal audit and review; who reads them, and when, is rarely stated.
themes.holders: Your team or project team (UK099); 'you' or organisations (UK174); not stated, nearest the organisation (UK268); organisations that use AI (UK010); public bodies (UK216); KIM teams (AI_Insights); the auditee, for work by external consultants (UK268); central government departments (UK136).
themes.binding: 'Must' in UK099 (226, 227, 269) in non-statutory guidance; 'should' and expected controls elsewhere; the EHRC presents record-keeping as good practice drawn from PSED case law. No consequences stated.
themes.checks: n/a (records support the checks described in other themes). Where stated, records are kept across the life cycle and updated regularly (inventory, assurance documentation).

themes.theme: Incidents, user reports and feedback: detection, investigation and response
themes.definition: Arrangements for collecting reports of problems from users and operators, detecting and logging incidents, investigating them and responding, including incident response plans.
themes.what_is_set_out: The Playbook (UK174) says, with 'must', that mechanisms be in place to investigate areas highlighted by users, and recommends nominating 'one or more SROs' to monitor reports and implement changes. UK099 asks for a feedback loop where users and operators can raise issues and for feedback to be broken down by group (its example, per the coder note, is a chatbot with 95% positive feedback where the question is who makes up the dissatisfied 5%). UK268 expects procedures for 'detecting, logging, and investigating incidents' and for security incidents including rollback; UK010 (Ofgem) asks for 'response plans for potential AI-related incidents'. UK071 is the most practical: in-interface flags such as 'this output seems wrong', logging every error with its root cause (example resolution within 48 hours for priority-one incidents, per coder note), documenting each incident, and an incident response plan that answers who investigates, what triggers rollback and when public disclosure is needed, although the answers are left to the team. AI_Insights asks that each bias incident be recorded with its triggering metrics, response, root cause and preventive measures, and suggests end users of live systems can correct the AI's errors; reporting deadlines and external notification do not appear in this cell.
themes.holders: SROs nominated by the body (UK174); 'you' or the team (UK099); the organisation (UK268); stakeholders (UK010); not stated, nearest the team (UK071, AI_Insights); end users (AI_Insights); central government departments (UK136).
themes.binding: UK174 'must' (041) in non-statutory guidance; otherwise 'should', recommended imperatives, 'core practice', 'possible control'. No consequences stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: user reports, interface flags, complaints, detected incidents, logged errors. Compared against: not stated. Metric or threshold: UK071 examples (incidents per period, mean time to detection and resolution, resolution within 48 hours for priority one); otherwise not stated. Who: SROs, the team, or not stated. What happens with the result: investigation; changes or decommissioning (UK174); rollback; records for post-incident review and learning.

themes.theme: Data protection impact assessment and data protection by design
themes.definition: Duties, mostly restated from UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018, to assess and control the personal-data risks of AI tools: DPIAs, data minimisation, purpose compatibility, privacy by design and handling of personal data held in models (split from the starting code 'impact assessment').
themes.what_is_set_out: This is the most legally grounded theme in the cell. The Playbook (UK174) restates that 'Article 35(3)(a) of the UK GDPR requires you to undertake a DPIA' where AI involves, among other things, profiling with legal or similarly significant effects or large-scale special-category data (coder note), lists ten DPIA steps, and restates data minimisation, purpose compatibility and a narrow ‘zone of recognition’ for biometric capture. The DWP policy (UK190) makes its DPIA process mandatory for users and for suppliers through their contract manager, with triggers that include using 'the output of an AI tool in a way that will affect people' (coder note to 171). UK206 states that 'All systems using personal data must carry-out a data protection impact assessment', whereas UK174 and UK099 tie the duty to the Article 35 triggers or to processing 'likely to result in a high risk', and AI_Insights says KIM teams 'should consider' a DPIA [inference: the documents do not agree on when a DPIA is required]. UK268 adds that a DPIA should show that less risky alternatives were considered and that the contribution of personal data to model performance should be measured, for example by retraining with less of it. UK099 and UK010 (Ofgem) add privacy by design, treating models trained on personal data 'as though they potentially contain personally identifiable data', and considering data removal before building or buying AI because removal from a trained model is not practical (coder note to 279).
themes.holders: 'You' or organisations developing and deploying AI (UK174, UK099, UK206); users and suppliers and their third parties (UK190); the Commissioner for data protection role (UK268) and DWP's Data Transfer Team; NAO for itself; KIM professionals (AI_Insights); teams (UK071); organisations completing ATRS records (UK086); central government departments procuring AI (UK136).
themes.binding: Statutory duties restated from UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 (UK174, UK099, UK206, UK268); 'must' as departmental policy (UK190); 'should' or 'consider' elsewhere. UK174 notes that data protection is 'a legal issue, with potentially serious consequences' (if-not-met field of 025), and UK268 names the risk of failing to comply with data protection law (if-not-met field of 087).
themes.checks: Trigger: before implementing or processing; where processing is likely to be high risk; on a change of purpose; before opening a dataset; before starting an AI-enabled review (KIM); before procurement. Compared against: UK GDPR principles; less risky alternatives; purpose-compatibility criteria (expectations of data subjects, type of data, impact, safeguards). Metric or threshold: necessity, proportionality, minimum data; UK071 example PII detection accuracy of 99% or more (coder note to 355). Who: 'you'; users; suppliers via the contract manager (UK190). What happens with the result: safeguards and technical and organisational measures put in place; the DPIA is recorded and listed in the ATRS record.
